narrative:
Your promotion is being denied because the model estimates a 52% chance that you will leave, meaning it sees you as slightly more likely to depart than to stay. This is not a certainty, but it is high enough that the organization treats you as a retention risk rather than a safe promotion investment.

The strongest factor in the model was your overall work experience, which actually pushed toward staying, not leaving. At one to five years, you match the most common experience range among employees predicted to stay, so this part of your profile is not the reason for the leave signal. The second and most important factor pushing toward leaving was that you have received other job opportunities while in this role. That is unusual: fewer than one in four employees predicted to stay had outside opportunities, so the model reads this as a clear sign of mobility. Your lack of medical insurance was the third factor, and it slightly pushed toward staying, likely because many stayers also lack that benefit.

Taken together, the model still lands just above the leaving threshold because your outside opportunities signal is strong, even though your experience and insurance profile partly offset it. Before making a final promotion decision, the organization should discuss your career path, pay, benefits, and recognition openly, because denying a promotion may itself increase your intention to leave. You should clarify what promotion would require and whether your current role meets those criteria.
